narrative: From Hundred Years’ War and Reconquista finales through Italian Wars, Ottoman–Habsburg collision, Reformation fracture, and the Dutch Revolt’s edge—Europe’s map is dynastic and confessional, not national.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.description: From Charles VII’s reconquest to Louis XI’s ruthless statecraft, France claws back English footholds, absorbs Burgundian wreckage, and draws Brittany into the crown’s orbit. Charles VIII’s and Louis XII’s Italian adventures export French arms into the peninsula and import Italianate taste to Fontainebleau. Francis I and Henry II duel Charles V’s encirclement; after mid-century the realm fractures in the Wars of Religion—Guise zeal, Huguenot resistance, and St Bartholomew’s blood. Henri of Navarre’s conversion, coronation, and Edict of Nantes (1598) close the century with a reunited Catholic monarchy that tolerates a guarded Protestant minority. Parlements, royal fiscal-military growth, and a Paris-centered court remake the medieval patchwork into an early modern state—still short of Louis XIV’s later frontiers.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War vs England (to 1453); Armagnac–Burgundian civil strife; League of the Public Weal; Burgundian succession wars after 1477; Italian Wars vs Habsburgs (1494–1559); Habsburg encirclement under Charles V/Philip II; French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) including St Bartholomew; interventions in Scotland and the Dutch Revolt; Franco-Spanish frontier fighting into 1600.
polities.leaders: Charles VI; Charles VII; Joan of Arc (captain of the sacred campaign); Louis XI; Charles VIII; Louis XII; Francis I; Henry II; Catherine de’ Medici; Charles IX; Henry III; Henry IV of Navarre/Bourbon.
polities.religion: Catholic monarchy with stubborn Gallican claims over papal interference. Calvinist Huguenots build consistories and noble clienteles from the 1550s; ultra-Catholic Guise leagues answer with Rome and Spain. The Edict of Nantes (1598) grants fortified coexistence without surrendering the crown’s Catholic public face.
polities.culture: Late Gothic piety yields to Fontainebleau’s Italianate court, vernacular chronicle, and print-shop politics. Royal entries, châteaux along the Loire, and a developing absolutist ceremonial teach subjects to see the king as the realm’s center. Occitan south remains culturally distinct under northern political victory; provincial parlements guard local privilege even as taxes centralize.
polities.summary: Valois France exits the Hundred Years’ War as a bruised but consolidating territorial monarchy. Charles VII and Louis XI claw back English footholds, break Burgundian autonomy, and absorb Brittany by marriage. Sixteenth-century kings fight…
polities.story: Joan of Arc’s 1429 Loire campaign and Charles VII’s consecration at Reims turn a disinherited Valois claim into sacral recovery; Formigny and Castillon (1450–53) end English Gascony. Louis XI outmaneuvers the League of the Public Weal and, after Nancy (1477), scavenges Burgundian spoils while Mary of Burgundy’s Habsburg marriage steals the Netherlands. The Italian Wars begin as dynastic opportunity and become a Habsburg–Valois meat grinder; Pavia (1525) captures Francis I and advertises Spanish tercios. Confessional civil war after 1562 makes every governorship a fortress: Coligny’s murder and the August 1572 massacres poison trust for a generation until Nantes trades coexistence for obedience.
polities.literature: Froissart’s afterlife and Commynes’ memoirs harden political prose; Rabelais carnivalizes learning; the Pléiade (Ronsard, du Bellay) elevates French verse. Montaigne’s Essays invent the self as a field of inquiry; d’Aubigné’s Tragiques remember confessional war in verse of ash and scripture.

polities.ideas: Gallicanism argues a French church under the crown; Bodin’s Six Books of the Republic theorizes sovereignty amid civil war. Politiques invent confessional truce as reason of state—order before purity—paving Henri IV’s settlement.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.description: England opens 1400 still claiming the French crown; Castillon (1453) ends the continental dream as the Wars of the Roses consume the nobility. Henry VII and Henry VIII rebuild monarchy on stronger fiscal and statutory footing; the break with Rome nationalizes the church and dissolves monasteries. Mary’s Catholic restoration fails to reverse the Protestant settlement that Elizabeth crafts after 1559. The Armada year (1588) and Irish wars advertise a naval-commercial kingdom projecting into the Atlantic while Calais—the last French bridgehead—falls in 1558. By 1600 Shakespeare’s London and the East India Company’s charter sit atop a still-fragile Tudor state awaiting James VI’s personal union.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War finale; Wars of the Roses; Anglo-Scottish wars (Flodden side); Tudor reconquest and plantation pressures in Ireland; war with Spain (Armada 1588); continental interventions in the Dutch Revolt and French Wars of Religion; Pilgrimage of Grace and other Tudor rebellions.
polities.leaders: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Edward VI; Mary I; Elizabeth I; ministers Wolsey, Cromwell, Cecil, Walsingham.
polities.religion: Late medieval Catholicism with Lollard undercurrents yields to Henrician schism, Edwardian Protestantism, Marian restoration, and Elizabethan settlement—a via media enforced by Uniformity, with Puritan pressure and Catholic recusancy as permanent tensions. Vernacular Bible and Book of Common Prayer reshape literacy and identity.
polities.culture: Print, parish literacy, and the Book of Common Prayer reshape speech and week. Tudor court humanism, London theaters, and joint-stock venturing invent a commercial-political public. Sumptuary display and progresses teach loyalty as spectacle.
polities.summary: Lancastrian England opens the century still claiming the French crown; defeat in France (1453) coincides with the Wars of the Roses. Tudor consolidation under Henry VII and Henry VIII remakes church and state—Break with Rome, dissolution of…
polities.story: Agincourt (1415) is the high theatrical crest of Lancastrian France; Joan of Arc and Charles VII erase it within a generation. Towton, Tewkesbury, and Bosworth turn succession into slaughter until Henry Tudor marries the rose factions together. Henry VIII’s matrimonial crisis becomes a constitutional revolution: supremacy statute, dissolved abbeys, and a Bible in English. Elizabeth’s regime survives northern Catholic revolt, Mary Stuart’s claim, and Philip II’s Armada—then spends blood and treasure on Ireland’s Nine Years’ War.
polities.literature: Malory compiles Arthurian loss; Tyndale’s Bible vernacularizes scripture; Spenser allegorizes empire in The Faerie Queene. Marlowe and Shakespeare make the history play a national mirror; by 1600 the stage is England’s loudest political philosophy.

Royal supremacy over the church; parliamentary statute as instrument of Reformation; Foxe’s martyrology as Protestant national memory; Hakluyt’s promotional geography for empire.
polities.ideas: Common-law constitutionalism and parliamentary statute become tools of Reformation. Richard Hooker defends an English church of reason and order; Hakluyt sells overseas expansion as Protestant duty.

polities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
polities.description: The Auld Alliance binds Scotland to France against England; Flodden (1513) guts a generation of nobles around James IV. Minorities, regencies, and English Rough Wooing keep the realm unstable until the Reformation Parliament of 1560 overturns the old church. Mary Queen of Scots’ Catholic personal rule ends in deposition and English captivity; her son James VI learns kingcraft as a Protestant monarch. In 1603 he inherits England—personal union, not incorporating union—while Highland and Borders worlds still run on kinship and raid.
polities.conflicts: Border wars with England; Flodden (1513); Rough Wooing; internal magnate feuds; Reformation crisis and Marian civil wars; involvement in French and English politics.
polities.leaders: James I–VI Stewarts; regents Albany and Morton; Mary Queen of Scots; John Knox (prophetic opposition); Bothwell; leading earls (Huntly, Moray).
polities.religion: Late medieval Catholicism yields to a Calvinist Reformation unusually thorough in kirk structure—presbyteries, Book of Discipline—while James VI fights for royal episcopal control. Highland Catholicism and older saints’ cults persist unevenly.
polities.culture: Lowland Scots literary culture; Highland Gaelic society; university towns (St Andrews, Glasgow, Aberdeen); martial borderer tradition; French cultural traffic via Auld Alliance.

polities.story: Flodden’s billhooks end James IV’s Renaissance chivalry in a single afternoon. John Knox’s return and the Lords of the Congregation pull Scotland into Geneva’s orbit; French troops and English intervention make reform a geopolitical bargain. Mary’s marriages, Darnley’s murder, and Langside ruin turn queenship into cautionary epic. James VI’s theoretical absolutism in True Law of Free Monarchies collides with kirk discipline—and then with English crowns.

polities.name: Crown of Castile
polities.description: Castile’s fifteenth century opens with noble civil war and weak kings (John II, Henry IV) before Isabella’s contested accession. Her partnership with Ferdinand of Aragon (1479) does not erase Castilian law or Cortes, but it pools armies for Granada’s conquest (1492). That year also launches Atlantic projection and the expulsion of Jews—twin signatures of a confessionalizing crusader crown. After 1500 the map’s Spanish Monarchy polity carries the dynastic union; Castile remains its tax base, infantry reservoir, and language of empire.
polities.conflicts: Reconquista vs Granada; civil wars among Castilian nobility; Portuguese border wars (including 1475–79 succession war); dynastic contests preceding Isabella.
polities.leaders: John II; Álvaro de Luna; Henry IV; Isabella I; Ferdinand (as consort in Castile); cardinal Mendoza; Columbus as crown agent.
polities.religion: Militant Catholic frontier faith; establishment of the Spanish Inquisition (1478) under royal control; pressure on conversos; endgame against Nasrid Islam; 1492 expulsion of Jews from Castile–Aragon.
polities.culture: Castilian vernacular rise; court chronicles; Mudéjar artistic hybridity; crusading frontier ideology; sheep-and-wool (Mesta) economy underwriting expansion.

polities.story: Isabella’s marriage is a coup against partition: Castilian succession crisis resolved by a partnership that still keeps realms plural. The War of Granada is slow siegecraft—artillery, starvation, and vassal bargaining—until Boabdil yields the Alhambra. Columbus’s first voyage, funded in the afterglow of that victory, redirects Castilian crusading energy westward. The Inquisition, already active before 1492, becomes a tool of confessional uniformity as empire expands.
polities.literature: Jorge Manrique’s Coplas mourn estate and death; romancero ballads recycle frontier war; Nebrija’s grammar (1492) claims language as empire’s companion.

polities.name: Crown of Aragon
polities.description: Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, the Balearics, Sardinia, Sicily, and (under Alfonso V) Naples form a contractualist thalassocracy as much as a land kingdom. Alfonso the Magnanimous’s Neapolitan court is an early Renaissance node; Catalan and Aragonese merchants stitch the western Mediterranean. Ferdinand II’s marriage to Isabella links crowns without dissolving fueros and Corts. After 1500 the Spanish Monarchy entry represents the dynastic union on the map, but Aragonese constitutional memory remains a brake on Castilian uniformity.
polities.conflicts: Italian ambitions vs Angevins and Italian states; Mediterranean rivalry with Genoa and later Ottomans; Castilian alliance politics; baronial and urban revolts within the crowns.
polities.leaders: Ferdinand I of Aragon; Alfonso V the Magnanimous; John II; Ferdinand II the Catholic; Germaine of Foix (brief second marriage politics).
polities.religion: Catholic composite with strong papal diplomacy; Inquisition extended; Mudéjar and Jewish communities under increasing pressure paralleling Castile.
polities.culture: Catalan-Aragonese commercial urbanism; Mediterranean court culture at Naples; contractualist political tradition (fueros/Corts); Catalan and Aragonese vernaculars beside Latin chancery.

polities.story: Compromís of Caspe (1412) shows elective-contractual habits inside dynasty. Alfonso V’s conquest of Naples exports Iberian power into Italian Wars’ prelude. Ferdinand’s Italy and Navarre policies braid Mediterranean strategy with Castilian armies. Germanías and local revolts remind rulers that Valencia and Catalonia are not silent provinces.

polities.name: Nasrid Emirate of Granada
polities.description: Paying parias and playing Castilian factions against each other, the Nasrids sustain a refined court under existential siege. Internal coups (Abu l-Hasan, Boabdil, al-Zagal) weaken resistance just as Isabella and Ferdinand unify Christian pressure. The war of 1482–92 is a sequence of sieges; the Alhambra’s surrender closes al-Andalus as a political project. Mudéjar and Morisco afterlives continue under Christian rule, but the emirate itself exits the map.
polities.conflicts: Defensive wars and raids vs Castile; dynastic coups inside the Nasrid house; final war of Granada (1482–1492) with systematic Castilian siege trains.
polities.leaders: Yusuf I and Muhammad V (earlier florescence still defining the palace); Muley Hacén; Boabdil (Muhammad XII); rival clan factions (Abencerrajes in legend).
polities.religion: Sunni Islam of a frontier emirate; Sufi currents; dhimmi Christian and Jewish communities under rising pressure as Castilian war intensifies; post-1492 forced conversions loom just beyond the surrender.
polities.culture: Nasrid palace culture—court etiquette, gardens, Arabic poetry—under siege; bilingual frontier; craft luxury as soft power when hard power fails.
polities.summary: Last Muslim polity on the Iberian Peninsula, paying parias and playing Castile against itself from the Alhambra. Internal Nasrid factionalism and Castilian–Aragonese unity under the Catholic Monarchs end the emirate in 1492—closing eight ce…
polities.story: The Alhambra’s inscriptions call itself a pearl—architecture as theology of paradise under pressure. Boabdil’s factional captivity and restoration become Castile’s lever; Málaga and Baza fall to artillery and hunger. 2 January 1492: keys change hands; within months Columbus sails and Sephardic expulsion begins—Granada’s end as Europe’s hinge year.

polities.name: Spanish Monarchy (Castile–Aragon / Habsburg Spain)
polities.description: Ferdinand and Isabella’s union, Granada’s fall, and Charles V’s Burgundian-Habsburg inheritance create a monarchy spanning Iberia, Italy, the Netherlands, and the Americas. Philip II rules from the Escorial as bureaucratic-Catholic absolute theater; Lepanto (1571) crowns naval crusade, while the Armada (1588) and Dutch Revolt expose limits. The Iberian Union (1580) adds Portugal’s empire under one Habsburg without erasing Portuguese law. On this atlas Iberia, Italian holdings, and—mapped separately—the Netherlands show European weight; silver pays tercios until credit cracks.
polities.conflicts: Italian Wars; Comuneros revolt; Ottoman Mediterranean war (Lepanto 1571); Dutch Revolt; Anglo-Spanish War; interventions in French Wars of Religion; Morisco revolt (Alpujarras).
polities.leaders: Joanna and Philip the Handsome (succession bridge); Charles V; Philip II; dukes of Alba and Parma; Don John of Austria (Lepanto).
polities.religion: Tridentine Catholicism as state identity; Spanish Inquisition; Jesuits; mystics (Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross); expulsion pressures on Moriscos; zero tolerance for Protestantism at home.
polities.culture: Siglo de Oro beginnings—painting, mysticism, picaresque prose—funded by American treasure and Italian/Flemish connections; court etiquette of the Escorial age.

polities.story: Charles V’s imperial election (1519) makes Spain the purse of a universal Habsburg claim; comuneros learn the cost. Philip II annexes Portugal, builds the Escorial, and tries to strangle Dutch rebellion and English Protestantism in one strategic breath. Lepanto briefly sacralizes Mediterranean victory; the Armada’s wreck sacralizes English deliverance. Morisco revolt (1568–71) shows unfinished conquest inside Spain itself.
polities.literature: Lazarillo de Tormes and the picaresque; mystical prose and poetry; chronicles of the Indies; by 1600 Cervantes is writing toward Don Quixote (1605).

polities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
polities.description: Ceuta (1415), Madeira/Azores settlement, African gold and enslaved labor, Bartolomeu Dias’s Cape rounding, and Vasco da Gama’s India voyage (1498) invent a seaborne empire of feitorias. Cabral’s Brazil landfall and the Estado da Índia make Lisbon a spice capital. Sebastian’s disaster at Alcácer Quibir (1578) orphans the dynasty; Philip II wins the 1580 succession. Through 1600 Portugal stays mapped as itself—laws, language, and Asian networks under Habsburg kings.
polities.conflicts: Castilian wars (1385 aftermath memory); Moroccan campaigns (Alcácer Quibir 1578 disaster); competition with Ottomans and later Dutch/English in Asia; 1580 succession war.
polities.leaders: John I; Henry the Navigator (prince); Afonso V; John II; Manuel I; John III; Sebastian; Henry the Cardinal-King; Philip I of Portugal (Philip II of Spain).
polities.religion: Catholic crusading ethos redirected to Africa and Asia; Inquisition from 1536; Jesuit missions (Xavier) as Portuguese soft power; forced conversion pressures on Jews/conversos.
polities.culture: Age of Discoveries chronicles; Manueline architecture; maritime commercial elite oriented to Africa/Asia rather than European land war; Goa and Lisbon as imperial poles.
polities.summary: Aviz Portugal pioneers Atlantic exploration—Ceuta (1415), African coasts, Vasco da Gama’s India route (1498), and a seaborne empire of feitorias. European mainland borders stabilize after Aljubarrota’s memory; the 1580 succession crisis bri…
polities.story: Henry the Navigator’s myth packages Atlantic learning, crusade, and commercial reconnaissance. polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.description: From late Luxemburg/Habsburg emperors through Charles V, the Reich remains a legal-political order of estates, not a centralized kingdom. Imperial cities, electors, and territorial princes bargain via diets; the Golden Bull’s skeleton still structures elections. Luther’s revolt (1517+) and the Peasants’ War, then princely Protestant leagues, split the Empire confessionally; Augsburg 1555 freezes cuius regio. Ottoman pressure on the southeast and French pressure on the Rhine frame imperial politics until 1600’s uneasy calm before the Thirty Years’ War.

polities.name: Crimean Khanate
polities.description: Hacı Giray’s house builds a successor of the Golden Horde’s western wing under Ottoman protection after mid-fifteenth century. Slave raids deep into Ruthenia and Muscovy structure the steppe economy; Bakhchysarai courts Ottoman style. Alliances with Istanbul make Crimea the northern claw of Ottoman strategy. Coastal cities and interior herds form a dual ecology.
polities.conflicts: Raids on Muscovy and Lithuania/Poland; wars coordinated with Ottomans; rivalry with other Horde successors; Cossack counter-raids.
polities.leaders: Hacı I Giray (founder memory); Mengli I Giray; Devlet I Giray; later Giray khans under Ottoman investiture.
polities.religion: Sunni Islam; Ottoman caliphal prestige; dhimmi/ransom economies involving Christian captives; Sufi presence in towns.
polities.culture: Steppe nomadic-aristocratic society with fortified coastal cities; slave-trade economy; Giray court ceremonial; Crimean Tatar language and law.
polities.summary: Ottoman vassal Tatar khanate controlling Crimea and raiding deep into Poland-Lithuania and Muscovy. Successor fragment of the Golden Horde’s western wing; essential to Black Sea slave-trade and steppe diplomacy—Bakhchysarai’s court between…
polities.story: Annual slaughters and slave raids (yasyr) reach Moscow’s outskirts and Galicia; khanates play Ottoman, Muscovite, and Commonwealth patrons. The burning of Moscow’s suburbs (1571) under Devlet I Giray scars Ivan IV’s reign—steppe power still lethal.

polities.name: Principality of Wallachia
polities.description: Wallachia pays tribute and rebels in cycles—Mircea the Elder, Vlad Dracul, Vlad Țepeș, and later Neagoe Basarab navigate suzerainty. Ottoman pressure intensifies after mid-century; boyar factions invite foreign backing. Michael the Brave briefly asserts wider ambitions around 1600. Orthodox monasteries anchor culture under political instability.
polities.conflicts: Ottoman wars and tribute politics; Hungarian overlordship contests; raids with/against Moldavia; Michael the Brave’s unification wars (~1599–1601).
polities.leaders: Mircea the Elder (memory); Vlad II Dracul; Vlad III Țepeș; Neagoe Basarab; Michael the Brave; Ottoman-appointed princes.
polities.religion: Orthodox princely church; fortified monasteries as treasure houses and refuges; patriarchal ties to Constantinople under Ottoman umbrella.
polities.culture: Orthodox princely courts; fortified monasteries; frontier military society; Romanian vernacular rising beside Church Slavonic.
polities.summary: Danubian principality oscillating between Hungarian and Ottoman suzerainty. Vlad III Țepeș’s resistance becomes legend; by 1600 Wallachia is an Ottoman tributary with brief assertive moments under Michael the Brave, who briefly unites the t…
polities.story: Vlad Țepeș’s forest of stakes—terror as anti-Ottoman strategy—enters European broadsheets as monstrosity and later vampire myth. Michael the Brave’s 1600 entry into Alba Iulia briefly stitches Wallachia, Transylvania, and Moldavia—then assassination returns the map to tributary fragments.

polities.name: Principality of Moldavia
polities.description: Alexander the Good and especially Stephen III (1457–1504) make Moldavia a fortress of Orthodoxy against Ottomans, Hungary, and Poland. Vaslui (1475) advertises resistance; later rulers become Ottoman tributaries with Polish interference. Bucovina’s painted monasteries turn theology into exterior fresco for the laity. Buffer identity between steppe and Carpathians defines the polity.
polities.conflicts: Wars with Ottomans, Wallachia, Hungary, and Poland; vassalage struggles; Crimean and steppe raids across the Dniester.
polities.leaders: Alexander the Good; Stephen III the Great; Petru Rareș; later Ottoman-era princes; boyar factions.
polities.religion: Orthodox monastic revival under Stephen; painted monastery spirituality; ties to Athos and Constantinople; resistance identity as Christian antemurale.
polities.culture: Orthodox monastic culture; boyar politics; buffer identity between steppe and Carpathians; Church Slavonic then Romanian.
polities.summary: Eastern Carpathian–Dniester principality under Stephen the Great resists Ottoman absorption longer than many neighbors, then becomes a tributary. Cultural flowering of painted monasteries (Voroneț and kin) makes Moldavia’s sacred art a Euro…
polities.story: Stephen the Great’s forty-seven churches for forty-seven victories—piety as after-action report—define a reign of almost continuous war. Painted monasteries turn exterior walls into open-air Bibles; Ottoman suzerainty arrives without erasing that visual theology.
polities.literature: Chronicles of Stephen’s reign; liturgical manuscripts; later Romanian texts; diplomatic Slavic correspondence with Poland and the Porte.

polities.name: Golden Horde (late / Great Horde)
polities.description: Tokhtamysh’s earlier wars with Timur leave a weakened steppe empire. Fifteenth-century succession strife produces Crimean, Kazan, Astrakhan, and Great Horde fragments. Akhmat Khan’s stand on the Ugra (1480) fails to restore suzerainty over Moscow; by 1502 Crimea destroys the Great Horde’s remnant. The map’s Horde is a fading claim more than a stable empire.
polities.conflicts: Internal succession wars; Timur’s devastation aftermath; wars with Muscovy and Lithuania; rivalry with Crimean Khanate; final destruction early 16th century.
polities.leaders: Tokhtamysh (earlier memory); Ahmed Khan; various short-lived khans of the Great Horde; Crimean rivals who inherit the western claim.

polities.culture: Steppe imperial remnants; tribute politics; Turko-Mongol aristocratic tradition; caravan and raid economies.
polities.summary: Fragmenting Jochid successor still claiming suzerainty over Rus’ princes into the 15th century. Great Stand on the Ugra (1480) symbolizes Muscovy’s emancipation; the Great Horde collapses under Crimean and Muscovite blows by the early 1500s…
polities.story: After Timur’s earlier devastation, the Horde never fully reknits. Ahmed Khan’s retreat from the Ugra without battle becomes Muscovy’s freedom myth; Crimean Girays and Russian cannon finish the Great Horde. A steppe empire ends as paperwork of tribute and memory.
